Synagogue
SIN-uh-gog
noun (biblical institution)
From Greek synagōgē ("a gathering, assembly"), from synagō, "to bring together." The local assembly and meeting-house of the Jews for the reading and exposition of the Scriptures, prayer, and instruction.

See also: Synagogue

📖 Biblical Definition

The synagogue (Greek synagōgē, "assembly") was the local gathering and meeting-house of the Jewish people for the public reading and exposition of the Scriptures, prayer, and instruction — an institution that arose, most scholars hold, during or after the Babylonian exile, when the people, cut off from the temple, gathered to hear and study the Law. By the time of the New Testament, synagogues existed in every Jewish town in the land of Israel and throughout the dispersion, and they were central to Jewish religious life alongside the one temple at Jerusalem. The synagogue's service centered on the Word: the reading of the Law and the Prophets, followed by exposition and exhortation, with prayers and the recitation of the Shema. Its officers included the ruler of the synagogue, who oversaw the service, and the attendant who handled the scrolls. The synagogue is of great importance in the Gospels and Acts: the Lord Jesus "taught in their synagogues" throughout Galilee (Matt 4:23) and read and expounded Isaiah in the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4:16-21); the Apostle Paul made the synagogue his first stop in city after city, reasoning from the Scriptures with Jews and God-fearing Gentiles (Acts 13:14; 17:1-2; 18:4). The synagogue thus became, by God's providence, the seedbed of the early church's mission: a network of gatherings centered on the Scriptures, where the gospel could be proclaimed from the very texts that pointed to Christ. The Christian assembly inherited the synagogue's pattern of Word-centered worship — the reading and exposition of Scripture, prayer, and the gathering of God's people — even as it added the ordinances and the new-covenant gospel. The very word synagōgē is used once of a Christian assembly (James 2:2).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The local Jewish assembly and meeting-house for the reading and exposition of Scripture, prayer, and instruction (Greek synagōgē); arose around the exile; central in the Gospels (the Lord taught in synagogues) and Acts (Paul's first stop); the seedbed of the early church's Word-centered worship.

SYNAGOGUE, noun. Greek synagōgē ("assembly"); the local Jewish gathering and meeting-house.

For the public reading and exposition of the Scriptures, prayer, and instruction; arose around the Babylonian exile.

Central to Jewish life alongside the one temple; existed in every town and throughout the dispersion by the New Testament era.

The Lord Jesus taught in the synagogues (Matt 4:23; Luke 4:16-21); Paul made it his first stop in each city (Acts 13:14; 17:1-2).

The seedbed of the early church's mission and the pattern for Word-centered Christian worship; the word is used of a Christian assembly at James 2:2.

📖 Key Scripture

Luke 4:16-17 — "And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up: and, as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read. And there was delivered unto him the book of the prophet Esaias."

Acts 17:1-2 — "Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where was a synagogue of the Jews: And Paul, as his manner was, went in unto them, and three sabbath days reasoned with them out of the scriptures."

Matthew 4:23 — "And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing all manner of sickness and all manner of disease among the people."

Nehemiah 8:8 — "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The synagogue is corrupted when reduced to mere Jewish background, when its Word-centered pattern is forgotten by churches that displace preaching with spectacle, or when the "synagogue of Satan" rebukes (Rev 2-3) are misread as warrant for hatred of the Jewish people.

expand to see more

Word-centered pattern forgotten. The synagogue centered its gathering on the reading and exposition of Scripture — the pattern the Christian assembly inherited (Acts 17:2; 1 Tim 4:13, "give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine"). Churches that have displaced the preaching and exposition of the Word with entertainment, spectacle, or therapeutic talk have departed not only from the apostolic pattern but from the synagogue pattern that preceded and shaped it. The centrality of the read-and-expounded Word in Christian worship is not negotiable cultural preference; it is the inheritance of the people of God from the synagogue through the apostles.

Synagogue-of-Satan misreading. The risen Lord, in the letters to the seven churches, twice speaks of those who "say they are Jews, and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan" (Rev 2:9; 3:9) — a rebuke of specific hostile assemblies persecuting the church, claiming covenant standing they had forfeited by rejecting their Messiah. This phrase has been wickedly misused to justify hatred and persecution of the Jewish people as such. That is a gross corruption. The Lord Jesus was a Jew who taught in the synagogues; the apostles were Jews; salvation is of the Jews (John 4:22); and Paul's heart's desire and prayer was for the salvation of his kinsmen (Rom 10:1). The rebuke of specific hostile assemblies is no warrant for antisemitism, which Scripture nowhere sanctions and the gospel everywhere opposes.
